meta.ogDescription: Genuine Ayn Rand: from her essay "America's Persecuted Minority: Big Business" in Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal (1966), p. 61. Popular versions trim the opening words.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Rand’s essay “America’s Persecuted Minority: Big Business,” collected in Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal (1966), p. 61. The original sentence begins “Remember also that…”; the popular version leaves that out.

source.excerpt: Remember also that the smallest minority on earth is the individual. Those who deny individual rights, cannot claim to be defenders of minorities.
trail: Wikiquote’s Ayn Rand page ↗ lists the full sentence in its sourced section for Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal (1966), cited to Ch. 3, “America’s Persecuted Minority: Big Business,” p. 61.
The Ayn Rand Lexicon ↗ gives the same two sentences under “Minority Rights,” also cited to the essay in Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, p. 61.

The Ayn Rand Institute’s page for the essay ↗ says it is based on a lecture at the Ford Hall Forum, Boston, on December 17, 1961, and at Columbia University on February 15, 1962. The page says the essay was published by the Nathaniel Branden Institute in 1962 and later collected in Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal.
A Harvard Crimson report ↗ on the Ford Hall Forum talk summarizes her claim that “The American businessman is a persecuted minority.” The report does not quote the “smallest minority” line.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from an essay first published in 1962 and collected in Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal (New American Library, 1966). Both dates are well after 1931, so in the United States the text is under copyright, held by Rand’s estate and her publisher. A short quotation like this one is normally fair use.

author.name: Ayn Rand
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Born Alice O’Connor, Ayn Rand was a Russian-American novelist and philosopher. She founded Objectivism, a philosophy built on reason, self-interest and individual rights. Besides her novels The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged, she wrote many political essays. Her 1960s essay collections, including The Virtue of Selfishness and Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, are the source of many of her most-quoted lines on rights.

misattribution.heading: What gets mixed up
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Rand is sound. What goes wrong is the wording, and which Rand work people cite for it.

items.why: The sentence as printed begins “Remember also that the smallest minority on earth is the individual,” and has a comma after “individual rights.” Quote sites drop both. The meaning is unchanged (Wikiquote ↗).

Her essay “Collectivized ‘Rights’” in The Virtue of Selfishness (p. 104) has a related aside: “(and the smallest minority on earth is the individual).” It does not contain the second sentence about “defenders of minorities” (Ayn Rand Lexicon: Individual Rights ↗). A citation to that book for the two-sentence quote points to the wrong passage.

items.who: The December 1961 Ford Hall Forum lecture
items.why: The essay is based on that lecture (ARI ↗), but no transcript we checked shows the sentence was said aloud that night. Cite the printed essay, not the speech.

misattribution.truthLine: Ayn Rand wrote it, in “America’s Persecuted Minority: Big Business,” Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal (1966), p. 61 (Ayn Rand Lexicon ↗).

context.heading: Why she wrote it
lead: The essay’s argument is narrower than the quote suggests when it stands alone. Rand said that “liberal” intellectuals defended racial and religious minorities while ignoring “that small, exploited, denounced, defenseless minority which consists of businessmen.” Her target was antitrust law (Ayn Rand Lexicon, p. 44 ↗).

The “smallest minority” sentence comes near the end of that argument and pushes it as far as it goes: if minority rights matter, the individual is the smallest minority of all. Taken out of its setting, the line now circulates widely as a general statement about individualism and group rights.
